items.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
items.snippet: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.

items.title: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why
items.snippet: Scientists may have finally explained why up to more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from rocks around the world. New research suggests that powerful currents deep inside the planet slowly raised and lowered entire continents, allowing erosion to erase vast stretches of geological history before they were buried and preserved.

items.title: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors
items.snippet: A major breakthrough in superconductivity research has revealed that one of the essential ingredients for electricity to flow without resistance can exist at room temperature. Scientists discovered that electrons can form stable pairs at much higher temperatures than previously understood, suggesting that a different obstacle may be preventing room-temperature superconductivity.

items.title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
items.snippet: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support.

items.title: 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert
items.snippet: A remarkable 125,000-year-old discovery in Saudi Arabia reveals that early humans once thrived beside enormous lakes filled with wildlife in what is now a vast desert. Thousands of stone tools and ancient plant remains suggest these prehistoric people used sophisticated hunting techniques, potentially including weapons enhanced with poisonous plant compounds.
